How the methods work, in plain language

Reem's focus is IFS-informed EMDR: EMDR run with parts awareness, so the protective parts of you get consulted rather than overridden. It sits alongside two other approaches. Somatic Experiencing works with the nervous system directly, in small doses, to widen what you can tolerate. NARM works with the patterns that formed in childhood and how they still shape your present. Brainspotting comes in where it helps.

The four methods

NARM

The NeuroAffective Relational Model. Where a lifelong pattern was learned, how it was serving you, and whether it still is.

Somatic Experiencing

What the body is still holding, approached in doses small enough to integrate rather than flood.

EMDR

Finishing the processing of experiences stored raw, with stabilization first. EMDR certified, EMDRIA Approved Consultant.

IFS-informed EMDR

Where most of the work happens. For developmental trauma, and for EMDR that has stalled, flooded or gone nowhere.

Brainspotting and BASE-P come in where they help, and are not separate courses of treatment so much as alternate routes when the main ones will not settle.

How they fit together

They are not four separate treatments you pick between. In practice they interlock: NARM asks what pattern is running and where it was learned, Somatic Experiencing sets the pace your nervous system can hold, and IFS-informed EMDR does the processing once the first two have made room for it.

Which one leads on a given day depends on what you arrive with. A week of acute stress calls for stabilization. A recurring relational pattern calls for curiosity. A memory that keeps intruding calls for processing, once the parts holding it are on board.

You do not have to sort yourself into the right method before making contact. That is what the consult is for.

What the first weeks tend to look like

No two courses of therapy run the same way, and this is a shape rather than a schedule. It is here because "we will work with what you bring" is true and tells you nothing about what you are agreeing to.

The consult
Fifteen minutes, free. What is going on, what you have already tried, and whether this is the right practice at all. It ends in a referral elsewhere if that is the honest answer.
The early sessions
History-taking and preparation, which is where Reem's emphasis sits. Nothing gets opened in the first hour.
Before any processing
Somatic Experiencing builds the footing, in doses small enough to integrate. Any part of you with an objection to the whole project gets consulted rather than argued with.
Processing
When the protective parts agree to it, rather than when the protocol says it is time. How long that takes varies, and arriving slowly is not a delay.
Underneath all of it
NARM, tracking the pattern rather than the incident, for as long as the work lasts.

Some of this happens outdoors rather than on a screen: walk and talk therapy on a trail, and equine sessions near Dripping Springs.

Questions about the methods

Which method will Reem use with me?

Whichever the week calls for. She is a NARM therapist, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner and EMDR certified, so the approaches move with what you bring rather than being chosen in advance. NARM tracks the pattern, Somatic Experiencing sets the pacing, IFS-informed EMDR handles processing when there is room for it.

Do the methods get used in the same session?

Often, yes. They are not sequential modules. A single session can start with noticing what the body is doing, name the pattern that showed up, and end without processing anything at all if that is what the day holds.

Why not just do standard EMDR?

For a single discrete trauma with a stable nervous system, standard protocol often works well. When trauma is developmental and layered, parts of you have organized around keeping it away, and processing that skips those parts tends to flood, stall or stop working. Consulting them first is slower at the start and faster overall.

What is Brainspotting, and where does it fit?

An approach that uses fixed eye position to access where material is held, developed out of EMDR practice. Here it is an alternate route rather than a main one: useful when EMDR targeting will not settle, or when a client processes more easily without the back-and-forth of bilateral stimulation.
